question: Give an example of defending a decision when key stakeholders disagreed.

raiseTranscript.text: On my first project, I chose to use a simpler logging library even though the senior engineer wanted a more feature-rich one. I walked through the trade-offs on performance and onboarding time for the two new hires on the team.
What did the stakeholders say?
They pushed back hard in the design review. I pulled the actual numbers on startup time and showed we could add the missing feature later without blocking the launch.
How did it end?
We shipped on time and the team later thanked me for keeping scope small. I learned to bring data earlier next time.

raiseNotes: Q: Give an example of defending a decision when key stakeholders disagreed.
Role: new grad on first project; chose simpler logging lib vs senior engineer preference
Actions: brought startup-time numbers and onboarding impact to design review
Outcome: shipped on schedule; later added feature without delay
Quote: "I pulled the actual numbers on startup time and showed we could add the missing feature later"
Follow-up: Asked what pushback looked like → candidate described concrete metrics used
junior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for junior. The candidate defended a scoped decision with measurable trade-offs rather than opinion. Quote shows they used data on startup time to address the senior engineer's concern. Story stays within individual scope and demonstrates coachability when they note learning to bring data earlier. Biggest strength is willingness to surface numbers instead of deferring to seniority.

lowerTranscript.text: I wanted to use the new framework but the tech lead said no. I kept explaining why it was better but they still said no so we used the old one.
I just did what they said. I didn't really have more data so I dropped it.

lowerNotes: Q: Give an example of defending a decision when key stakeholders disagreed.
Role: new grad; wanted new framework but tech lead overruled

Outcome: complied without further input; no measurable impact shown
Quote: "I just did what they said. I didn't really have more data so I dropped it."

junior.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for junior. Candidate described a preference rather than a defended decision and stopped after the first objection. Quote reveals they had no data to counter the tech lead. Story shows compliance instead of ownership or learning. Biggest gap is lack of attempt to quantify trade-offs or revisit after gathering evidence.

raiseTranscript.text: I decided to keep the existing payment service instead of building a new one, even though product and finance both wanted a custom solution for a new market.
How did you handle the disagreement?
I ran a two-week spike, shared latency and cost projections across three markets, and showed the custom path would delay launch by eight weeks with only marginal revenue upside in year one.
What was the result?
Both teams agreed to the phased approach. We launched on time and later measured the actual revenue delta was within 5% of my projection.

raiseNotes: Q: Give an example of defending a decision when key stakeholders disagreed.
Role: senior; chose to reuse existing payment service vs product/finance custom build request
Actions: two-week spike with latency, cost, and revenue projections across markets
Outcome: secured agreement on phased rollout; launch on time; measured revenue within 5%
Quote: "I ran a two-week spike, shared latency and cost projections across three markets"
Follow-up: Asked about disagreement handling → candidate described cross-team data sharing
senior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for senior. Candidate used a time-boxed spike to generate cross-team data that changed the outcome. Quote shows they quantified delay and revenue impact rather than arguing preference. Story demonstrates influence without authority by bringing measurable trade-offs to product and finance. Biggest strength is closing the loop with actual post-launch measurement.

lowerTranscript.text: Product wanted a new feature but I knew it would break our SLAs so I told them we couldn't do it.
They escalated to my manager. I explained the risks again but didn't have a written trade-off so we ended up doing a smaller version later.

lowerNotes: Q: Give an example of defending a decision when key stakeholders disagreed.

Outcome: escalation occurred; smaller version shipped later without clear metrics
Quote: "I explained the risks again but didn't have a written trade-off"
Follow-up: Asked about escalation → candidate admitted lack of documented analysis
senior.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for senior. Candidate relied on verbal risk statements without data, leading to escalation. Quote highlights absence of written trade-offs. Story shows limited cross-team influence and no attempt to quantify the SLA impact or propose phased options early. Biggest gap is treating disagreement as a debate instead of a data exercise.

raiseTranscript.text: My team owned the recommendation engine. Marketing wanted us to prioritize a partner integration that would have cut our model accuracy by 12%.
What did you do?

I had the team run an A/B test on a small cohort, presented the accuracy drop and downstream revenue impact to the marketing and finance leads, and proposed a joint roadmap that kept accuracy while still meeting the partner deadline in Q3.
How did the team respond?
Marketing agreed to the phased plan. We protected the core metric and still delivered the integration. Two engineers on the team later used the same data-driven approach on their own projects.

raiseNotes: Q: Give an example of defending a decision when key stakeholders disagreed.
Role: manager; protected recommendation engine accuracy vs marketing partner integration request
Actions: ran A/B test, quantified 12% accuracy drop and revenue impact, proposed joint Q3 roadmap
Outcome: phased plan accepted; core metric protected; two engineers adopted the approach
Quote: "I had the team run an A/B test... and proposed a joint roadmap"
Follow-up: Asked about team response → candidate described engineers applying same method
manager.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for manager. Candidate protected a key metric while still delivering for a partner team through a data-backed compromise. Quote shows they used team resources to generate evidence and created a shared roadmap. Story illustrates leverage by teaching the method to engineers. Biggest strength is turning disagreement into a repeatable team practice.

raiseTranscript.text: We had to choose between two acquisition targets. The board and product org favored the larger one for market presence, but my analysis showed the smaller target had 3x higher strategic fit with our platform roadmap.
How did you defend it?

I created a 10-year NPV model incorporating integration cost, talent retention, and platform synergies, then ran a two-day offsite with the board and leadership to walk through scenarios. We ultimately acquired the smaller company and the platform team hit their three-year goals six months early.
What trade-offs did you surface?
The model showed the larger target would require a separate integration team for four years. That clarity let us reallocate those headcount dollars to product instead.

raiseNotes: Q: Give an example of defending a decision when key stakeholders disagreed.
Role: exec; chose smaller acquisition target vs board preference for larger one
Actions: built 10-year NPV model with integration cost and synergies; ran board offsite with scenarios
Outcome: smaller target acquired; platform goals hit six months early; headcount reallocated
Quote: "I created a 10-year NPV model incorporating integration cost, talent retention, and platform synergies"
Follow-up: Asked about trade-offs surfaced → candidate described four-year integration team requirement
exec.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for exec. Candidate used long-horizon modeling to shift board opinion on a high-ambiguity acquisition. Quote shows they quantified multi-year integration costs and talent impacts. Story demonstrates strategic judgment by converting disagreement into a shared scenario exercise that changed resource allocation. Biggest strength is linking the decision to three-year platform outcomes.

lowerTranscript.text: The board wanted the bigger acquisition. I presented my view but they went with the larger target anyway.
Did you do any follow-up analysis?
We moved forward. I didn't run additional scenarios after the decision was made.

lowerNotes: Q: Give an example of defending a decision when key stakeholders disagreed.
Role: exec; preferred smaller acquisition but board chose larger
Actions: presented view once; no extended modeling or scenario work after initial disagreement
Outcome: larger target selected; no post-decision analysis or reallocation shown

Follow-up: Asked about follow-up analysis → candidate stopped after initial presentation
exec.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for exec. Candidate presented a preference without sustained data or scenario work to influence the outcome. Quote shows they did not iterate after the board decision. Story lacks evidence of long-term strategic framing or trade-off clarity. Biggest gap is treating the disagreement as a one-time event instead of an opportunity to reshape the discussion.
